title: Elucidation and Development of Synthetic Receptor Mechanisms for Sensing Protein Ligands
abstract: Cell-based therapies are a promising technology for treating diseases, with approved clinical applications such as cancer immunotherapy. Such therapies necessitate the development of custom sense-and-respond functionality to extend cells’ ability to target specific physiological environments and disease states. To achieve this, synthetic receptors, such as Modular Extracellular Sensor Architecture (MESA), have been engineered to sense soluble ligands and cell surface markers. In MESA, each receptor comprises two transmembrane proteins that heterodimerize upon ligand binding to initiate intracellular signaling linked to downstream transcriptional outputs. Such biosensors rewire detection of extracellular ligands to production of a therapeutic protein. As with other engineered receptor systems, translation of MESA receptors to sense new targets of interest poses many challenges. Notably, many physiologically-relevant proteins like cytokines are typically multimeric in nature and much larger than small molecules sensed in model systems. Here, towards the goal of engineering versatile biosensors, dimerization propensities of MESA receptors are characterized using Förster resonance energy transfer, providing insights about receptor geometry for ligands of varying size. Building on these characterizations, a new MESA receptor mechanism that aims to overcome the identified challenges is explored. This new receptor design incorporates pre-formed receptor complexes that inhibit ligand-independent background signaling and receptor activation via the binding of large ligands that separate these pre-formed inhibitory complexes, enabling signaling. This new mechanism is tailored for large ligand targets and amenable to binding homodimeric ligands. This investigation has identified required features for engineered receptors to sense protein-based ligands and expands the therapeutic potential of cell-based therapies.
